cards.prompt: You type `example.org` into your browser. Before any packet can be sent to the website, what has to happen first?

options.text: DNS turns the name into an IP address
Routers read the name example.org to choose a route
The website encrypts its name so nobody can read it
Your home router gives example.org a private address

cards.explanation: Routers deliver packets using **IP addresses**, not names. So your device first asks **DNS** to turn example.org into an address, like looking up a number in a contacts app. Only then can packets be sent.

cards.prompt: Which of these names is controlled by whoever registered **example.org**?

options.text: news.example.org
example.org.news.example.com
example-org.example.net
news.example.org.example.net

cards.explanation: Read from the right. `news.example.org` ends in **example.org**, so it's a subdomain its owner added. The others end in `example.com` or `example.net`, so they belong to whoever registered those, even though they contain the words "example.org".

cards.prompt: Nobody has looked up example.com recently. Match each DNS server to what it would "say" during the lookup.

pairs.right: "Leave it with me, I'll find out for you."
"I don't know, but here are the .com servers."

cards.explanation: The **resolver** does the asking for you. The **root** server points to the `.com` servers, the **TLD** server points to example.com's own server, and only the **authoritative** server gives the real answer.

cards.prompt: A website will move to a new IP address in 10 minutes. Its DNS answers have a TTL of **3,600**. Will every device that has just looked it up switch to the new address as soon as it moves?

options.text: No: they may keep using the old answer for up to an hour
Yes: every cache is updated the moment the site moves
Yes: 10 minutes is longer than the TTL, so it runs out first
No: they'll keep the old answer forever, until restarted

cards.explanation: DNS TTLs are in seconds: 3,600 seconds is **one hour**. A device that has just cached the answer may keep it for up to an hour, which is longer than the 10 minutes before the move. Nothing tells caches that a site moved, but the answer isn't kept forever either. Website owners often lower the TTL before a move for this reason.

cards.prompt: Your browser looks up `shop.example.org`. The answer is a **CNAME** pointing to `example.org`. What happens next?

options.text: It looks up example.org to get an actual address
It connects to the name example.org straight away
It gives up, because the answer contained no address
It asks for shop.example.org's MX record instead

cards.explanation: A **CNAME** holds a name, not an address, and you can't connect to a name. So the lookup carries on with `example.org` until it finds an **A** record with a real address. MX records are about email, not websites.

cards.prompt: Run `nslookup example.org` and find its **IPv4** address.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Ask DNS for the address of example.org
commands.output:
Server:		127.0.0.53
Address:	127.0.0.53#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:	example.org
Address: 203.0.113.80
Name:	example.org
Address: 2001:db8::80

cards.explanation: example.org's IPv4 address is `203.0.113.80`. The other answer, `2001:db8::80`, is its IPv6 address, and `127.0.0.53` at the top is the DNS helper that answered the question.

cards.prompt: Visits to `example.org` go to one server, but email to `hello@example.org` goes to a different machine. How does DNS make that work?

options.text: One name holds an A record for the site and an MX record for email
The name holds a CNAME record that sends email to the website server
Email doesn't use DNS at all, so it finds its server another way
DNS can only hold one answer, so email must use a second domain

cards.explanation: One name can hold several **records**. The **A** record gives the website's address, and the **MX** record names the mail server, so the two jobs can go to different machines. A CNAME is just an alias to another name.
